summary: A status report on a proposed Data Reconfiguration Service, a network service to translate data from the form one computer produces into the form another expects. It covers the purpose, motivation and design so far. RFC 166 gives the implementation specification.

plainLanguage.summary: The Data Reconfiguration Service would translate data into the form a program expects. A programmer defines a named set of rules, and a user can later apply those rules to a data stream.

subtitle: A proposal for a network service that reformats data streams using stored forms.

tldr.problem: Programs and terminals on different hosts may expect different data formats, and changing every program to match one format can be difficult.
tldr.mechanism: A Data Reconfiguration Service stores named forms and applies their rules to data streams between a user process and a serving process.
tldr.outcome: RFC 138 describes a proposed experiment, requests comments, and reports that several sites planned experimental implementations.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 138 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The RFC describes an experiment and asks readers for comments.

sections.title: Why Reformat Data
sections.content:
RFC 138 argues that application programs need different input and output formats. It proposes adapting the Network to each program's needs instead of requiring every program to follow one format.

A programmer would define a form describing a transformation. The service would store the form under a name so a later user could call it while processing a Network data stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Different programs can expect data to be arranged in different ways. The proposed service would apply a saved recipe to change that arrangement.

sections.title: The Service Connections
sections.content:
The proposal describes a control connection between the originating user and the service, a user connection between a user process and the service, and a server connection between the service and a serving process. A form is defined over the control connection and applied to data passing over the other two.

The user can define, list, or remove forms and can request simplex or duplex connections between processes.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection carries instructions to the service. Two other connections carry data between the user's program, the service, and the serving program.

sections.title: Rules in a Form
sections.content:
The Form Machine reads an input stream, applies an ordered set of rules, and produces an output stream. A rule can compare input, assign or reuse values, and emit data in another form; if a match fails, the machine can try another rule.

The proposal defines bit-string, octal, hexadecimal, EBCDIC, and Network ASCII data types, along with control options for moving between rules or returning from a form. Examples include inserting fields, deleting data, reordering fields, and converting characters.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is a list of matching and rewriting rules. The service reads part of the input, decides which rule applies, and writes the transformed output.
